title: The Road from Rose Lawn: chickens, shop windows, two editorials, and the Land of Oz
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Rose Lawn and the Weak Heart

stops.name: Chittenango, the birth into oil and barrels
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The coordinate is corrected: the geography lens carried 43.0466, -75.8646, about 0.8 km off Wikipedia's figure for the village, and the afterlife lens already used the corrected value.
stops.campa: Lyman Frank Baum is born on the fifteenth of May in Chittenango, seventh of the nine children of Benjamin Ward Baum and Cynthia Ann Stanton Baum. The father has made money in oil and in barrel-making, and the household is Methodist and comfortable. The blood is German, Scots-Irish, and English. The village will one day pave a stretch of its sidewalk yellow on his account and open a museum of his props. For now it is a canal town in Madison County, and the newest Baum is one more child in a house that can afford him.
suggested_refs: The Erie Canal village of Chittenango, Madison County, New York

stops.name: Rose Lawn, Mattydale: tutors instead of a schoolroom
stops.date_confidence: the residence is attested for roughly 1858 to 1873; no month or day is given anywhere and the date is defaulted. The coordinate is corrected from the pool's 43.0912, -76.1355 to Wikipedia's figure for Mattydale, about 1 km northwest.
stops.campa: The family moves to a rural estate outside Syracuse that they call Rose Lawn, and here the boy grows. He is reputed to have a weak heart, so he is not sent to a school; tutors come to the house and teach him alongside his brothers and sisters. He reads what he likes and wanders where he likes. He will describe the place afterward as a paradise and will spend forty years building versions of it out of paper. The estate footprint is gone. The ground under it now carries a middle school on Roxboro Road.
suggested_refs: The site of Rose Lawn, now occupied by Roxboro Road Middle School, Mattydale

stops.name: Peekskill Military Academy, the heart that stops over a daydream
stops.date_confidence: the enrollment is attested to about age twelve and lasts roughly two years; no month is given. The coordinate is corrected to the academy's own site at Elm and Hudson Streets, replacing the pool's downtown-Peekskill placeholder.
stops.campa: At about twelve he is sent down the Hudson to Peekskill Military Academy at the corner of Elm and Hudson Streets, where the discipline is hard and daydreaming is punished. Under it his body gives out. Biographers call the collapse a psychogenic heart attack, a heart stopping for reasons that are not in the heart. He is withdrawn after roughly two years and never attends another school. The academy keeps him on its list of notable alumni and closes in June 1968, a century after he arrived at its gate.
suggested_refs: Peekskill Military Academy, founded 1833 as Peekskill Academy, closed June 1968

stops.name: Mattydale, the press his father buys him
stops.date_confidence: the amateur journals are attested to the 1870s and The Stamp Collector to about age seventeen, that is 1873; no month or day exists for either and 1870 is the opening of the range.
stops.campa: His father buys him a small printing press, and Frank and his brother Henry Clay Baum begin issuing amateur journals from Rose Lawn, among them The Rose Lawn Home Journal. By seventeen he has founded a philatelic paper called The Stamp Collector and is dealing stamps on the side. The press is a toy and he works it as a business. He does the same thing again with poultry in 1880 and with department store windows in 1897: take up an enthusiasm, then print the paper for the people who already share it.
suggested_refs: Surviving numbers of The Rose Lawn Home Journal and The Stamp Collector

stops.name: Syracuse, the dry goods counter and the fancy Hamburgs
stops.date_confidence: the clerkship is placed at about 1875 to 1880 and the poultry breeding at about age twenty; neither carries a month. The Poultry Record is attested to March 1880 and is folded into this stop rather than given a pin of its own, since the pool names only 'New York State'.
stops.campa: He clerks in his brother-in-law's dry goods company in Syracuse, learning the counter and the stock book. At about twenty he takes up breeding fancy Hamburg chickens, a show breed with laced feathers, and in March 1880 he founds a trade paper for the fanciers called The Poultry Record. Neither the counter nor the coop holds him. The theater is what he wants, and his father, who has indulged every enthusiasm so far, is about to buy him one. The Hamburgs outlast the paper: his first book, six years off, is a manual on how to breed them.
suggested_refs: The Poultry Record, founded March 1880
Hamburg fowl of the laced show varieties

stops.name: Richburg, Baum's Opera House
stops.date_confidence: the pool dated the theater 1880; Wikipedia's Richburg article gives Baum's management of Baum's Opera House as 1881 to 1882 and the later date is used. The coordinate is corrected from the pool's 42.1231, -78.179, about 4.2 km off. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: Benjamin Ward Baum builds his son a theater in the oil town of Richburg, and from 1881 to 1882 Frank manages it, writes for it, and acts in it under two stage names, Louis F. Baum and George Brooks. He is twenty-five and running a house of his own in a boomtown. The oil under Allegany County pays for the building, the same trade that paid for Rose Lawn. It is the last thing his father's money buys him before the money goes, and he will not have a stage of his own again.
suggested_refs: Baum's Opera House, Richburg, Allegany County, 1881 to 1882

stops.name: Richburg, the theater burns in March
stops.date_confidence: March 1882 attested for the fire; no day. The pool's claim that the only script of The Maid of Arran perished with the building is struck as false and the reasons are printed in the campa.
stops.campa: In March the theater burns to the ground during a production of Baum's own play Matches. Costumes and scenery go with it. The story that the only manuscript of The Maid of Arran perished in the fire is repeated everywhere and is wrong: that play opens two months later and tours for a year, and its script survives with charred edges, written up afterward in the box office. The play genuinely lost at Richburg is The Mackrummins, which nobody has read since the night the roof came in.
suggested_refs: The burned site of Baum's Opera House, Richburg, March 1882

stops.name: New York, The Maid of Arran on his twenty-sixth birthday
stops.date_confidence: the premiere date of 15 May 1882 is attested, as are the two Broadway stints and the closing at Richmond, Indiana on 7 June 1883. The premiere venue is named in nothing reached, so the pin is the canonical New York coordinate inherited byte-identical from mark_twain.journey.json rather than an invented theater address.
stops.campa: On his twenty-sixth birthday The Maid of Arran opens, an Irish melodrama with songs for which Baum has written the book, the lyrics, and the music, and in which he plays Hugh Holcomb. It is the nearest thing to a hit he will have on a stage until Oz. The company tours through 1882 and 1883, twice into Broadway houses, and closes on the seventh of June 1883 at Richmond, Indiana. Nothing in the reachable record names the theater where the curtain first went up on it.
suggested_refs: The touring company of The Maid of Arran, 1882 to 1883

stops.name: Fayetteville, the parlor of Matilda Joslyn Gage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, with the officiant named.
stops.campa: On the ninth of November he marries Maud Gage in the parlor of her mother's house at Fayetteville, W. H. Hawley of the Fayetteville Baptist Church officiating. The mother is Matilda Joslyn Gage, who wrote the History of Woman Suffrage with Stanton and Anthony and who holds that the churches invented the subjection of women. She thinks little of actors and less of this one. She will die in her son-in-law's house, and it is her library and her argument that run under the country he has not invented yet.
suggested_refs: The Matilda Joslyn Gage House, Fayetteville, New York

stops.name: Shonnard Street, Syracuse: the first house and the first son
stops.date_confidence: the birth is attested to 4 December 1883 and the house to 1882 to 1884. No street number appears in any source reached, so the coordinate marks the historic street corridor and nothing narrower.
stops.campa: The newly married pair rent a house on Shonnard Street in Syracuse, their first address together, and on the fourth of December their first son, Frank Joslyn Baum, is born in it. The father is twenty-seven and has a touring company, a chicken paper, and no capital. The son will outlive him by decades and will one day rename what is left of his father's film studio. No street number survives in anything reachable, so this pin marks the corridor of the old street and admits it.
suggested_refs: The Shonnard Street corridor, west Syracuse

stops.name: Syracuse, the second son and The Book of the Hamburgs
stops.date_confidence: the birth is attested to 1 February 1886. The pool placed it at 28 Slocum Avenue, where the family moved on 1 May 1884; Wikipedia's Maud Gage Baum article places the birth at a Holland Street residence instead, for which the pool supplies no coordinate. The Slocum pin is retained and the conflict is left standing.
stops.campa: On the first of February the second son, Robert Stanton Baum, is born, and the birth leaves Maud with peritonitis that nearly kills her. The same year Baum publishes his first book, The Book of the Hamburgs, a manual on breeding a show chicken. It is not a fairy tale and it sells to fanciers, and it is the first time his name appears on a spine. Two sources put the family in two different Syracuse houses in these years, Slocum Avenue and Holland Street, and neither is dismissed here.
suggested_refs: The Book of the Hamburgs (1886), Baum's first published book

stops.name: Aberdeen, the family gets down from the train
stops.date_confidence: the pool carried both July 1888 and 20 September 1888. Wikipedia's Maud Gage Baum article is specific to the day for the family's arrival, and July at best marks Baum's own advance trip. The longitude is corrected from the pool's -98.4865, about 1.4 km off, on this and every other Aberdeen stop.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of September Maud, Frank, and their two sons come west to Aberdeen in Dakota Territory, where her sisters are already settled and where the railroad has been dropping new towns on the prairie for a decade. Statehood is thirteen months away. The country is in the last year of a wet cycle that has convinced everyone the rain follows the plow, and the town believes it is going to be a city. The Baums arrive at the exact top of the boom and will watch the whole of the bust.
suggested_refs: Aberdeen, Dakota Territory, in the last year before South Dakota statehood

stops.name: Baum's Bazaar on Main Street
stops.date_confidence: the opening is attested to 1 October 1888 and the failure to 1889 to 1890; the storefront address is not confirmed in anything reached, so the pin marks downtown Aberdeen. Harry Neal Baum's birth is corrected from the pool's 17 December to Wikipedia's 18 December 1889.
stops.campa: On the first of October he opens Baum's Bazaar on Main Street, a variety store of china, glassware, toys, and novelties, and he runs it the way he runs everything. He extends credit to farmers who cannot pay, tells stories to the children who come in for candy, and keeps the books badly. The drought arrives, the farmers do not pay, and within about a year the store is bankrupt. His third son, Harry Neal Baum, is born on the eighteenth of December 1889, in the middle of the failure.
suggested_refs: The Main Street storefront of Baum's Bazaar, Aberdeen

stops.name: The Aberdeen Saturday Pioneer, Our Landlady
stops.date_confidence: Baum's ownership and editorship of the Pioneer runs 25 January 1890 to 21 March 1891, tighter than the pool's bare '1890'. The office address is not recorded in anything reached.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of January he takes over a weekly newspaper, the Aberdeen Saturday Pioneer, and edits it for fourteen months. He writes a satirical column in the voice of a boarding-house keeper, Our Landlady, whose talk carries most of what he thinks about the town, about women's suffrage, and about what is coming. Matilda Joslyn Gage's arguments come through the column almost unaltered. It is the best writing he does before Chicago, and the paper is failing from the day he buys it.
suggested_refs: The Our Landlady columns, Aberdeen Saturday Pioneer, 1890 to 1891

stops.name: Grand River, Standing Rock: the killing he answers in print
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the death is placed between twelve and one in the afternoon. Baum is not present. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from sitting_bull.journey.json, where the atlas has already stood on this ground.
stops.campa: Three hundred miles east of Baum's desk, before dawn on the fifteenth of December, thirty-nine Indian police of the Standing Rock agency come to Sitting Bull's cabin on the Grand River to arrest him, and by early afternoon he is dead at his own door, shot by the same police sent to take him. The news reaches Aberdeen by wire within days. The Saturday Pioneer goes to press five days later, and what Baum writes about the killing is the reason this ground belongs in his own route at all.
suggested_refs: Sitting Bull's cabin on the Grand River, Standing Rock Reservation
sources: sitting_bull.journey.json, stops 'Grand River, thirty-nine police before dawn' and 'Grand River, the shots at the door'

stops.name: Aberdeen, the editorial of the twentieth of December
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, as printed in the Aberdeen Saturday Pioneer. The reception of the two editorials is contested among historians and that dispute is not adjudicated here; the text itself is not in dispute.
stops.campa: Five days after the killing, Baum prints an editorial in the Saturday Pioneer calling for the total annihilation of the few remaining Indians. He is thirty-four, bankrupt, editing a dying paper in a town that is emptying, and he writes that the safety of the settlers depends on wiping out the people whose ground they are standing on. It is the same hand that will write, ten years later, that the heartaches and the nightmares are to be left out. Both sentences are his, printed a decade apart, and neither erases the other.
suggested_refs: The Aberdeen Saturday Pioneer editorial of 20 December 1890
sources: Wikipedia, 'L. Frank Baum' (Aberdeen Saturday Pioneer editorial)

stops.name: Wounded Knee Creek, the ground under the second editorial
stops.date_confidence: the massacre is attested to the day. Baum is not present and no source places him here. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from low_dog.journey.json and sitting_bull.journey.json.
stops.campa: Fourteen days after Sitting Bull dies, the Seventh Cavalry surrounds Big Foot's people on this creek while they are being disarmed and kills some three hundred of them with rifle and Hotchkiss gun, more than half women and children. Baum is not here. Nobody in Aberdeen is here. The ground stands in his route only because five days later he sits at a desk in Aberdeen and writes about what happened on it, the second and last editorial he will ever publish on the subject.
suggested_refs: The mass grave on the hill above Wounded Knee Creek
sources: low_dog.journey.json, stop 'Wounded Knee Creek, the ground he is not standing on'

stops.name: Aberdeen, the second editorial and the end of the paper
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The pool's claim that the Pine Ridge and Standing Rock tribes formally sought a retraction in 2006 is inverted and is corrected here: what 2006 records is an apology by two Baum descendants.
stops.campa: On the third of January he prints the second editorial, repeating the call to wipe out what remains of the Native population, this time with the massacre already in the papers. Eleven weeks later, on the twenty-first of March, he gives up the Saturday Pioneer. In 2006 two of his descendants will apologize to the Sioux nation for what he wrote here. No retraction is ever issued by the paper, which is dead within the year, and none by the man, who leaves for Chicago and never comes back to Dakota.
suggested_refs: The Aberdeen Saturday Pioneer editorial of 3 January 1891
sources: Wikipedia, 'L. Frank Baum' (Aberdeen Saturday Pioneer editorial)

stops.name: Humboldt Park, Chicago: the fifth move
stops.date_confidence: the move is attested to 1891 with no month; April follows the sale of the Pioneer in March. The coordinate is corrected from the pool's -87.722, which falls west of the park's own edge. Humboldt Park's article makes no mention of Baum; the residence rests on the two Baum articles and the Chicago Literary Hall of Fame. The Theosophical membership of 1892 is [R], carried in Baum literature and not confirmed in anything reached this session.
stops.campa: The paper gone, the Baums move with their four sons to Humboldt Park on Chicago's northwest side, into a city rebuilding itself for the Columbian Exposition. He reports for the Chicago Evening Post, then goes on the road for a china and glassware house, carrying a sample case through the Midwest for years. In 1892 he is said to join the Chicago branch of the Theosophical Society, the movement Blavatsky founded in New York and Annie Besant carried on after her, a membership later biographers read straight into the cosmology of Oz.
suggested_refs: The Chicago Evening Post newsroom, 1891 to 1892
Pitkin and Brooks, Chicago china and glassware wholesalers
sources: Katharine M. Rogers, L. Frank Baum: Creator of Oz (2002), for the Pitkin and Brooks employment

stops.name: Chicago, Mother Goose in Prose and The Show Window
stops.date_confidence: both the book and the magazine are attested to 1897; neither carries a month. The coordinate is the canonical Chicago pin, inherited byte-identical from maurice_sendak.journey.json, otto_hanish.journey.json, and fyodor_yevtishchev.journey.json.
stops.campa: In one year he does two things. He founds The Show Window, the first trade magazine for department store window trimmers, and teaches shopkeepers how to build a lit box that stops a person on a sidewalk. And he publishes Mother Goose in Prose, nursery rhymes retold as stories, illustrated by Maxfield Parrish at the beginning of his career. Both are trades in display. The magazine outlives his editorship under a longer name, Merchants Record and Show Window, and the window trimmers keep his rules.
suggested_refs: The Show Window, later Merchants Record and Show Window
Maxfield Parrish's plates for Mother Goose in Prose (1897)

stops.name: 68 Humboldt Boulevard, Matilda Joslyn Gage dies in the house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Chicago's 1909 street renumbering makes the modern address uncertain, so the coordinate approximates the historic Humboldt Boulevard corridor.
stops.campa: Matilda Joslyn Gage dies on the eighteenth of March in her son-in-law's house on Humboldt Boulevard, where she has been living. She had told him for years that the stories he invented for his children were worth writing down. The suffragist who was written out of her own movement's history dies in the house where the Oz books are about to be written, and her daughter Maud will keep the family solvent for the next thirty years on the inheritance. Chicago renumbers its streets in 1909 and the address goes uncertain.
suggested_refs: The Humboldt Boulevard house, Chicago, pre-1909 numbering

stops.name: Chicago, Father Goose: His Book
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested, the month is not, and the day is defaulted. The Macatawa cottage purchase that follows is dated only to about 1900 to 1910 in the pool and is folded forward into the 1907 stop.
stops.campa: Father Goose: His Book appears, verses by Baum and pictures by W. W. Denslow, and it becomes the bestselling children's book of the year. It is the first money he has ever made from writing. He is forty-three and has been a chicken breeder, an actor, a shopkeeper, a newspaper editor, and a traveling salesman, and he has just found the trade he will die in. The proceeds buy a summer cottage on Lake Michigan at Macatawa Park, which he names Sign of a Goose and fits out himself.
suggested_refs: Father Goose: His Book (1899), Baum and Denslow

stops.name: 68 Humboldt Boulevard, the introduction dated April
stops.date_confidence: Baum signed the introduction 'Chicago, April, 1900' and the day is defaulted. The writing of the book at the Humboldt Boulevard house is attested by Wikipedia's Maud Gage Baum article.
stops.campa: He finishes the book in the house on Humboldt Boulevard and writes an introduction for it in April, signing it with the city and the month. In it he names Grimm and Andersen as the makers of the fairies that came before, then sets them aside: their tales carry heartaches and nightmares, and his will not. It is a modernized fairy tale, he writes, meant only to please, and he means the sentence as a manifesto, not a modest disclaimer, a deliberate break with the whole tradition he was raised reading.
stops.quote: Having this thought in mind, the story of "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz" was written solely to please children of today. It aspires to being a modernized fairy tale, in which the wonderment and joy are retained and the heartaches and nightmares are left out.
stops.quote_source: Introduction, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (Chicago, April 1900), George M. Hill Co.; text from Project Gutenberg ebook 55
suggested_refs: The signed introduction to The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chicago, April 1900
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 55, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz

stops.name: Chicago, George M. Hill prints ten thousand
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The pool's claim that both the first and second printings sold out by October 1900 is corrected: the first edition sold out, the second was 'nearly depleted' shortly after.
stops.campa: On the first of September the George M. Hill Company of Chicago publishes The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, with W. W. Denslow's pictures and Denslow's name on the copyright beside Baum's. The first printing of ten thousand copies is gone by October and a second printing of fifteen thousand is nearly gone behind it. It is the bestselling children's book of 1900 and again of 1901. Baum is forty-four. Every remaining year of his life will be spent inside the country he has just drawn.
stops.quote: Folklore, legends, myths and fairy tales have followed childhood through the ages, for every healthy youngster has a wholesome and instinctive love for stories fantastic, marvelous and manifestly unreal. The winged fairies of Grimm and Andersen have brought more happiness to childish hearts than all other human creations.
stops.quote_source: Introduction, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (Chicago, April 1900), George M. Hill Co.; text from Project Gutenberg ebook 55
suggested_refs: The George M. Hill Company first edition of 1900, co-copyrighted with W. W. Denslow

stops.name: New York, the musical runs two hundred and ninety-three nights
stops.date_confidence: the Broadway opening is attested to January 1903 and the run to 293 performances; no day is given and the venue is not named in the pool, so the coordinate is the canonical New York pin inherited byte-identical from mark_twain.journey.json.
stops.campa: With the composer Paul Tietjens and the director Julian Mitchell, Baum turns the book into a stage extravaganza with chorus girls, a live cow, and a plot loosened almost past recognition, and in January it opens on Broadway and runs two hundred and ninety-three performances. It returns the next year and tours the country until 1911. Mark Twain is in this city in these same years, another man who began in a printing shop and learned that the platform pays better than the page.
suggested_refs: The 1902 Tietjens and Mitchell stage extravaganza of The Wizard of Oz

stops.name: Chicago, The Marvelous Land of Oz
stops.date_confidence: the Author's Note is dated Chicago, June 1904; the day is defaulted.
stops.campa: He had meant to write one book. The letters come instead, thousands of them, children asking what happened next to the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, and in June Reilly and Britton publish The Marvelous Land of Oz with an Author's Note explaining that he is doing as he is told. He will keep doing as he is told for fifteen years, one Oz book most years, while every other scheme he attempts loses money. The children commission the series and the children keep it running.
stops.quote: After the publication of "The Wonderful Wizard of OZ" I began to receive letters from children, telling me of their pleasure in reading the story and asking me to "write something more" about the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman.
stops.quote_source: Author's Note, The Marvelous Land of Oz (Chicago, June 1904), Reilly & Britton; text from Project Gutenberg ebook 54
suggested_refs: The Author's Note to The Marvelous Land of Oz, Chicago, June 1904
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 54, The Marvelous Land of Oz

stops.name: Chicago, the Woggle-Bug closes and Pedloe Island is dropped
stops.date_confidence: the scheme and its collapse are attested to 1905 with no month. The pool gives the island's location only as 'off the California coast' and names no theater for the musical, so the pin is Baum's home city in 1905 rather than an invented California coordinate.
stops.campa: He plans an Oz amusement park on an island off the California coast that he calls Pedloe, a fairyland built to scale for children, and he stakes it on the success of a new stage musical, The Woggle-Bug. The musical fails. The island is dropped and no ground is ever bought. It is the first of the four ventures that will empty him, and the only one that would have put Oz on actual ground. Nothing reached this session names the theater where it closed.
suggested_refs: The Woggle-Bug, stage musical of 1905
The unbought Pedloe Island Oz park scheme

stops.name: Giza, the pyramids on the six-month tour
stops.date_confidence: the six-month expedition through Egypt, Greece, Italy, North Africa, Switzerland, and France is attested to 1906. The source names countries, never cities, so Giza is the standard Cairo itinerary point and the pin is [R]. Sorrento, Geneva, Athens, and Algiers were carried in the pool on the same reasoning and are dropped from this route as unlocated guesses; one representative pin is kept for the tour rather than six.
stops.campa: Baum and Maud take a six-month expedition through Egypt, Greece, Italy, North Africa, Switzerland, and France, and in Egypt they go out to the pyramids at Giza. He is fifty and has money for the first and the last time in his life. The source names the countries and not the cities, so this pin is the standard Cairo itinerary and nothing stronger than that. He comes home to write more Oz books and then to lose everything he has on a machine for projecting them onto a screen.
suggested_refs: The 1906 Baum expedition through Egypt, Greece, Italy, North Africa, Switzerland, and France

stops.name: Macatawa, the Sign of a Goose and the Author's Note
stops.date_confidence: the Author's Note to Ozma of Oz is datelined Macatawa 1907 with no month; June is a default within the summer season the cottage was used. The cottage's name is corrected from the pool's 'Sign of the Goose' to 'Sign of a Goose'. The coordinate is corrected from 42.7825, -86.2117, about 1.5 km north of the community.
stops.campa: At the Lake Michigan cottage he bought with the Father Goose money and named Sign of a Goose, Baum writes the Author's Note to Ozma of Oz and quotes his readers back at themselves, including one child who informs him which of his own inventions are properly Ozzy. Answering mail is a part of the job now. The Royal Historian title he adopts in 1910 is already implicit here: he does not claim to invent the country, only to receive dispatches out of it and set them down.
stops.quote: My friends the children are responsible for this new "Oz Book," as they were for the last one, which was called The Land of Oz. Their sweet little letters plead to know "more about Dorothy"; and they ask: "What became of the Cowardly Lion?" and "What did Ozma do afterward?"
stops.quote_source: Author's Note, Ozma of Oz (Macatawa, 1907), Reilly & Britton; text from Project Gutenberg ebook 33361
suggested_refs: The Sign of a Goose cottage, Macatawa Park, Michigan
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 33361, Ozma of Oz

stops.name: Chicago, The Fairylogue and Radio-Plays
stops.date_confidence: the show is attested to 1908 and to a touring circuit; the pool gives the place only as 'United States (touring)' and names no opening house, so the pin is the canonical Chicago coordinate and the September date is the season, not a documented opening night.
stops.campa: He builds a touring show that puts him on a stage in evening dress beside hand-tinted lantern slides and film of his own characters, live actors walking into the projected scenery, an orchestra under all of it. The Fairylogue and Radio-Plays costs more per night than any house can return, and the tour ends in the year it starts, having eaten the Oz royalties. Three years later he files for bankruptcy over the theatrical losses. Nothing reached this session names the theater where it opened or the town.
suggested_refs: The Fairylogue and Radio-Plays, hand-tinted slide and film tour of 1908

stops.name: Coronado, The Road to Oz
stops.date_confidence: the preface is datelined Coronado 1909 with no month. The visits are dated only to about 1904 to 1910. The coordinate is corrected from the pool's 32.6858, -117.183, about 0.65 km off Wikipedia's figure for the hotel. The Emerald City attribution is a live contradiction and is left standing.
stops.campa: He winters at the Hotel del Coronado across the bay from San Diego and does much of his writing at the hotel, the preface to The Road to Oz among it. The hotel says he modeled the Emerald City on its own white towers. Most of his biographers say he modeled it on the White City of the 1893 Chicago fair, which he was living beside at the time. Both claims are in circulation, neither is settled here, and the only man who could say died without saying it.
stops.quote: Well, my dears, here is what you have asked for: another 'Oz Book' about Dorothy's strange adventures. Toto is in this story, because you wanted him to be there, and many other characters which you will recognize are in the story, too.
stops.quote_source: "To my readers," The Road to Oz (Coronado, 1909), Reilly & Britton; text from Project Gutenberg ebook 26624
suggested_refs: The Hotel del Coronado, Coronado, California
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 26624, The Road to Oz

segments.name: Hollywood and the Oz Film Manufacturing Company

stops.name: Hollywood, the move west
stops.date_confidence: the move is dated about 1909 to 1910 with no month; the pool's competing claim of 1911 is the bankruptcy year, not the move. The coordinate is the canonical Hollywood pin inherited byte-identical from fritz_lang.journey.json and fyodor_yevtishchev.journey.json. The pool's description of Hollywood as a small independent town is corrected in the campa.
stops.campa: The Baums leave Chicago for Hollywood, driven west by his failing health. Hollywood is no longer the independent town the story usually makes it: it was voted into the City of Los Angeles on the seventh of February 1910, and the film business is only beginning to come out from the east coast. Fritz Lang will land in this same district thirty-four years later, out of a different ruin. Baum arrives with an Oz royalty, a wife with an inheritance, and debts he has not yet declared.

stops.name: Ozcot, the house Maud's inheritance builds
stops.date_confidence: the house is attested as custom-built in 1910 with Maud's inheritance; no month. The street address, 1749 N. Cherokee Avenue, is widely cited in Baum literature but appears in no source reached this session, and Wikipedia's own Ozcot article gives no address. The afterlife lens placed Baum's death at 34.0928, -118.3287 instead, about 1.2 km south; this file uses the Cherokee Avenue figure at every Ozcot stop and records the disagreement.
stops.campa: With Maud's inheritance from her mother the family builds a house on North Cherokee Avenue and calls it Ozcot. He keeps a chicken yard and a prize-taking dahlia garden behind it and covers one interior wall, the Yard of Maud, with photographs of his wife. It is the only house he ever owns outright, and it is in her name along with everything else, because the bankruptcy is a year off and he has already arranged for it not to reach her. The house is demolished decades after his death.
suggested_refs: Ozcot, Hollywood, built 1910, demolished in the mid twentieth century

stops.name: Chicago, the bankruptcy
stops.date_confidence: August 1911 attested; no day. The filing is placed in Chicago per the pool; the family is already living in Hollywood by then, which is why the route doubles back.
stops.campa: In August he declares bankruptcy over the theatrical losses, the Fairylogue chief among them. Having transferred the property to Maud in advance, he is left with his clothes, a typewriter, and his library, and he has also signed away the rights to his own early books, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz included. He is fifty-five. He goes back to California and writes another Oz book, and then another, and the royalties from the new ones keep up the house that belongs to his wife.
suggested_refs: The 1911 bankruptcy filing and the surrendered rights to the early Oz titles

stops.name: Santa Monica Boulevard, the studio between Gower and Lodi
stops.date_confidence: the founding is attested to 1914 with no month. The longitude is corrected from the pool's -118.313, about 1 km too far east, which lands near Van Ness rather than at the Gower and Lodi block.
stops.campa: He founds the Oz Film Manufacturing Company and builds a studio on Santa Monica Boulevard between Gower Street and Lodi Place, taking the office of president and doing the producing and the screenwriting himself, with Louis F. Gottschalk as vice president, Harry Marston Haldeman as secretary, and Clarence R. Rundel as treasurer. Three years after the bankruptcy the man is running a film studio. He is fifty-eight and he has learned nothing whatever about money.

stops.name: Santa Monica Boulevard, the company swallowed by Metro
stops.date_confidence: the failure is attested to 1915 with no month. The pool's claim that the company renamed itself Dramatic Feature Films is corrected: the renaming was done by Baum's son after the absorption by Metro Pictures.
stops.campa: The films get made and the exhibitors will not book them, because the trade has decided that pictures for children do not pay. Within a year the company fails and is absorbed by Metro Pictures. Baum's son Frank Joslyn Baum renames the remnant Dramatic Feature Films, a detail commonly and wrongly credited to Baum himself. The lot passes on to Famous Players-Lasky, which becomes Paramount, and the ground goes on making pictures for a century without him on it.

stops.name: Ozcot, the Royal Historian answers his mail
stops.date_confidence: The Magic of Oz is attested to 1919 and its preface is datelined Ozcot, Hollywood; no month is given and the day is defaulted. The preface was written during the final illness and the book appeared posthumously the same year.
stops.campa: He is in bed for most of the last year, and he writes to his readers out of it. In the preface to The Magic of Oz he apologizes for the letters he has not answered during a long and confining illness, promises to do better, and signs himself Royal Historian of Oz. He has written thirteen Oz books since the first and is finishing the fourteenth. The gall bladder surgery of the previous year has not held. He is drafting Glinda of Oz in a room in a house that belongs to his wife.
stops.quote: Assuring you that my love for you has never faltered and hoping the Oz Books will continue to give you pleasure as long as I am able to write them, I am Yours affectionately, L. FRANK BAUM, "Royal Historian of Oz."
stops.quote_source: "To My Readers," The Magic of Oz (Ozcot, Hollywood, 1919), Reilly & Lee; text from Project Gutenberg ebook 419

stops.name: Ozcot, the stroke
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: On the fifth of May he suffers a stroke at Ozcot and falls into a coma. He does not come out of it except in fragments. Glinda of Oz is finished on the desk and will not be published for fourteen months. The Magic of Oz is not out yet either; it will appear in the summer, carrying a preface written by a man who already knew. Maud is in the room. Forty-nine years earlier a boy with a reputed weak heart was pulled out of a military academy and sent home to Rose Lawn.

stops.name: Ozcot, the Shifting Sands
stops.date_confidence: 6 May 1919 is carried by the biography article and by every account reached. One passage in Wikipedia's 'Ozcot' article gives 16 May instead; the contradiction is recorded and not resolved. The reported last words are [R], a deathbed tradition with no independent witness.
stops.campa: He dies at Ozcot on the sixth of May, nine days short of his sixty-third birthday. The last words attributed to him, spoken to Maud, are Now we can cross the Shifting Sands, the deadly desert that seals off the Land of Oz on every side in his own books. The line is repeated in every account and rests on no independent witness, carried here as tradition rather than as verified speech. One passage in one article gives the death as the sixteenth of May. The sixth is carried everywhere else.

stops.name: Forest Lawn, Glendale: the grave
stops.date_confidence: the month is attested and the day is not. 8 May is set two days after the death so that the burial does not precede it; it is not a documented date. The coordinate reconciles the two lenses, which disagreed by about 1.9 km, on the afterlife lens's figure, which matches Wikipedia's for the cemetery.
stops.campa: He is buried at Forest Lawn Memorial Park in Glendale, on the far side of the hills from Hollywood, in the cemetery the film industry is starting to fill. Forest Lawn's own account of its notable dead does not list him; the confirmation comes only from his biography. The Wonderful Wizard of Oz has sold for nineteen years and will sell for a century more, and the man who wrote it dies owing money and owning a typewriter. Fritz Lang goes into the other Forest Lawn, in the Hollywood Hills, fifty-seven years later.

stops.name: Chicago, Glinda of Oz and the next Royal Historian
stops.date_confidence: the publication is attested to 10 July 1920. The place is given in the pool only as 'United States'; the pin is the canonical Chicago coordinate, Reilly & Lee being a Chicago house. Thompson's succession is attested to 1921 and the public-domain date to 1956.
stops.campa: Reilly and Lee publish Glinda of Oz on the tenth of July, fourteen months after his death, the last book in his own hand. The following year the publisher hires Ruth Plumly Thompson to go on being the Royal Historian of Oz, and she writes twenty-one more, seven beyond Baum's own count. The original book passes into the United States public domain in 1956, three million copies sold, and the adaptations stop needing anyone's permission. Alexander Volkov has by then already rewritten it in Russian as The Wizard of the Emerald City, with a girl named Ellie and a dog named Totoshka.

stops.name: Chittenango, the yellow brick sidewalk
stops.date_confidence: the sidewalk is attested to 1982 and its replacement to a 2007 revitalization; neither carries a month. The museum and the festival are attested without dates in the source.
stops.campa: The village where he was born paves a stretch of its downtown sidewalk in yellow brick. The bricks come up again in a 2007 revitalization and go back down as stamped and colored concrete, which is what happens to yellow brick roads. Chittenango also keeps the All Things Oz Museum, run by the International L. Frank Baum and All Things Oz Historical Foundation, with costumes and props from the 1939 film beside Baum family objects, and holds an Oz-Stravaganza festival on the first Friday and Saturday of June.

stops.name: Wounded Knee Creek, two descendants apologize
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested and nothing narrower is given. The location of the apology is recorded nowhere reachable; the pin is the canonical massacre coordinate, which is the ground the second editorial was pointed at, and is not a claim about where anyone stood.
stops.campa: In 2006 two of Baum's descendants apologize to the Sioux nation for the hurt their ancestor caused. Earlier accounts of this apology had it backwards, as a retraction demanded by the Pine Ridge and Standing Rock tribes; no such demand is documented anywhere, and the correction is printed here rather than buried. Where the apology was made is not recorded anywhere reachable. The pin marks the ground the editorials were pointed at, since that is the only place the record can honestly stand it.

stops.name: Chittenango, the Yellow Brick Road Casino
stops.date_confidence: the casino opening is attested to 2 June 2015. The Chicago Literary Hall of Fame induction is attested to 2013 and is folded into this stop rather than given a separate pin. The claim that the book exists in 56 languages is dropped: that figure is in no source reached, which says only 'nearly every major language'.
stops.campa: On the second of June the Oneida Indian Nation opens the Yellow Brick Road Casino near Chittenango, themed on The Wizard of Oz, a hundred and twenty-five years after the editorials in Aberdeen. Two years earlier Baum was inducted into the Chicago Literary Hall of Fame for the Humboldt Park years. Both facts stand recorded side by side, neither one cancelling the other. The book is in nearly every major language; some Indian editions replace the Tin Woodman with a horse, and Hebrew editions call the country Eretz Uz, after the land in the book of Job.

stops.name: Bronxville, an address he never had
stops.date_confidence: not a biographical date. This is the date of compilation, and the stop exists to record an unsupported claim rather than to place Baum anywhere. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from the interlock lens's Bronxville pin; the afterlife lens gave 40.9387, -73.8326, a difference of about 25 metres, and that disagreement is recorded too.
stops.campa: No source places Baum living in Bronxville, New York, despite a claim that put him there. His documented addresses across sixty-two years form their own itinerary instead: Chittenango, Mattydale, Peekskill, Syracuse, Richburg, Aberdeen, Chicago, Macatawa, Coronado, and Hollywood, a restless circuit driven by bankruptcy, failed ventures, and his own bad heart chasing warmer winters at the end. Bronxville's own published list of notable residents does not carry his name, and no biography or city directory puts him on any street there. The pin marks a claim, not a life; the life ran through ten other towns first.
